Jordan answered fast: "Ours, obviously, it's for our class." Priya sent a shrug emoji. Mya tried a different approach, the way she'd test a rule in science: collect data. She messaged her uncle, her grandmother, and Lena's mother, asking each one what their family called the country in their own language.

The answers came in through the evening. Her grandmother wrote back a whole text about the village, and then added, "Here we say it our way, there they say it theirs, both are true names." Lena's mother sent one line: "Deutschland, always." Mya copied the messages into a document for her citation page, so her teacher could see where each name came from. She noticed a pattern: every family member used their own word, and not one of them used the English one, unless they were talking to someone outside.

"So which one wins?" Jordan asked, when she posted her draft. He still wanted his slide first and had moved on to arguing about presentation order, but Priya had gone quiet, and then sent: "Wait. My mom calls our family's country something different too. I just never thought about it. Can I put both on my page?"

Mya looked at Lena, who was leaning in the doorway in her borrowed sweatpants, reading over her shoulder. Lena tapped the screen where Mya had typed both names side by side, then the two labels underneath them. "A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym," Lena said, "and a name outsiders use is an exonym." Mya added the last line to her poster and hit send. Priya replied within a minute: "Doing it. Mine's going up first, Jordan."

"Fine," Jordan typed. "But I'm still going before the bell invades my free time."

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: Teasing often depends on an audience, so walking away with the targeted classmate, saying something like "Come on, let's go," can end it without a confrontation.
story:
Hazel stood on the back porch of Marisol's birthday party holding a paper with six numbered lines on it, because tomorrow she had to run the first Nature Club meeting of the year and she had never run anything except a lemonade stand that failed. Marisol had offered her party as a practice audience. "Pretend we're the club," Marisol said, waving a forkful of cake at the six kids scattered around the porch. "You be the conductor."

"Conductor of what?" asked Theo.

"Of the meeting," Hazel said. "Like an orchestra, except with people who all want to talk about salamanders at once." She read the first line of her agenda. "Item one: does anyone actually want to sell candy at the fall fair, or was that just Mr. Ruiz's idea?" It went surprisingly well for two items. Priya argued, Dev made a joke about the treasurer's report, but everyone got a turn, and Hazel started to believe she could do this.

Then item three fell apart because of the laughing.

A boy named Quinn was standing near the snack table, and two kids from another school, Rex and some kid Hazel didn't know, were circling him. "Nice shoes," Rex kept saying. "No, really. Nice shoes." They said it in that voice that meant the opposite, and Quinn's ears went red, and every time Rex spoke, the second kid laughed like a drum machine.

Hazel's first idea was to say something sharp to Rex. She even opened her mouth. But then she noticed something she couldn't see directly, only its shadow: Rex kept glancing sideways before each joke, checking whether the porch was still watching. It was like watching a performer count his audience. The laughing kid was the audience. Take away the audience, she thought, and what's left?

She revised her plan mid-breath. "Quinn!" she called, loud and casual. "Come on, let's go. I need help with the snacks in the kitchen." Quinn blinked, then pushed off the table and followed her through the screen door. Rex opened his mouth for another "nice shoes," but there was nobody left to hear it except his one friend, and somehow that wasn't enough. When Hazel peeked back through the window thirty seconds later, Rex was standing there looking bizarre, like a magician whose trick had ended early, and then he wandered off toward the bounce house.

In the kitchen, Quinn dumped chips into a bowl without being asked. "Thanks," he said. "That was getting old."

"That's the whole trick, I think," Hazel said. "They need people watching. No watchers, no show." She looked at her agenda, all six items, and realized item three had taught her more than items one and two put together. Tomorrow she would write the meeting plan differently, with room for whatever actually happened. "Okay, back to the porch," she said. "We never settled the candy question, and I still have three items left. Bring the chips."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Young bones generally heal faster than adult bones, so children usually spend less time in a cast than adults with a similar break.
story:
Brody sat on the flat wooden bench behind the baseball diamond, his right arm sweating inside its white cast. Six weeks, the doctor had said, and that was two weeks ago. Across the field, Coach Delgado was running drills, and Brody watched every throw like he could absorb it through his eyes.

His grandfather lowered himself onto the bench beside him with a grunt. Grandpa's left wrist wore a cast too, tan colored and dented at the thumb. "Ten weeks for me," Grandpa said, wiggling his fingers. "You'll beat me out of mine by a month, I'd wager."

Brody frowned. Same kind of break, he knew that much. He had been there in June when Grandpa tripped on the porch step, and three weeks later Brody had landed wrong diving for a line drive, and the x-rays had looked almost identical, side by side on the light board. Same bone, same crack, same doctor. So why ten weeks for Grandpa and six for him?

That was the question he turned over all through batting practice. It was plausible that the doctor just liked kids better, but that seemed weak. It was plausible that Grandpa's break was secretly worse, except the x-rays had matched. Brody liked explanations he could test.

So he tested one. At halftime of his sister's soccer game the next Saturday, he walked the sideline with a notebook and asked every person he could find who had ever broken a bone: how old were you, and how long was the cast on. Marcus, age twelve, five weeks. Marcus's mom, age thirty-eight, nine weeks. The referee had broken his ankle at forty-five and spent three months in a boot. By the end of the afternoon Brody had twelve names, and the pattern jumped right off the page. Every kid was out of a cast faster than every grown-up.

He showed the notebook to his grandfather on Sunday. Grandpa read it slowly, tapped the column of numbers, and laughed. "Young bones heal faster than old ones. Kids spend less time in a cast than adults with the same break." He shook his head. "Sixty-eight years old and learning it from a thirteen-year-old with a notebook."

The day Brody's cast came off, the nurse cut it away with a little buzzing saw and let the sunlight expose his pale, skinny arm to the air for the first time in a month. It looked strange, like it belonged to a younger kid. Outside, Grandpa was waiting in the truck with the window down and the ball bag already loaded.

"Think that arm still works?" Grandpa asked.

Brody rolled down the window the rest of the way, picked up a baseball from the seat, and fired it straight into his grandfather's glove.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Nervousness triggers the release of adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach, causing the "butterflies" feeling.
story:
The parking lot was already half full when Adam's mom pulled up beside the gym doors, and his heart started hammering before he even touched the door handle. His stomach flipped too, like something small was doing somersaults in there, and he frowned at his own hands because they wouldn't hold still.

"You okay?" his mom asked.

"Fine," Adam said, which was mostly true. He wanted to go in. He'd wanted to go all week, ever since Priya said she'd save him a dance. So why was his body acting like he was about to be chased by wolves?

His best friend Dex came jogging across the lot, holding his phone up like a trophy. "Mr. Holloway let me plug into the speakers for two songs. Two! I'm basically the DJ generator of this whole dance. If those songs go over, he said maybe homecoming."

"That's huge," Adam said, but his stomach flipped again, harder.

Dex squinted at him. "Dude, you look like you're going to throw up on that car."

"I'm not nervous," Adam said. "That's the weird part. I want to be in there." Then he thought about it, turning it over the way he turned over a math problem. His heart was racing. His stomach felt wrong. If it were actual fear, wouldn't he want to leave? But he wanted to stay. So maybe the nervous part came first, even before he felt nervous, and the rest of him was just catching up. He'd read something once about butterflies, and now he tested it out loud: "Maybe it's just butterflies."

"Butterflies," Dex repeated, nodding like a scientist. "Nervousness gives you that. Your heart goes fast and it pulls blood away from your stomach, so it feels like that."

"So if I get my heart to slow down, the butterflies quit?" Adam didn't wait for an answer. He breathed in slow through his nose, out slow through his mouth, four times, while Dex watched with the fascinated horror of someone seeing a friend do something embarrassing in public.

Halfway through the fifth breath, Adam realized his stomach had stopped flipping. His heart still beat fast, but it was the good kind now, the kind that came from the music leaking out under the gym doors and the laughing inside and the fact that in about nine minutes he would be standing in front of Priya.

"Okay," he said, and pulled his jacket tighter even though it was too thin to insulate him from the October cold. "Let's go make you famous."

Dex's grin was infectious. He shoved his phone in his pocket and pushed through the doors first, and Adam followed him straight into the noise and the lights.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: After the climax, the falling action and resolution show the consequences of what happened and tie up the story's loose ends.
story:
Claire kept a systematic list in her notebook titled "What Makes a Story Work," and so far it had three items: dialogue goes in quotation marks, each new speaker gets a new paragraph, and something big has to happen near the end. Today was the read-aloud in Mr. Reyes's room, and she had signed up first.

Her story was about a dog named Biscuit who slipped his leash and ran into the woods behind the school. In her favorite part, the narrator waded through brush and found Biscuit hiding under a log covered with a shelf-like fungus, trembling but safe. She had checked every line of dialogue twice. "Come here, boy," the narrator called. "It's okay." Commas, quotation marks, new paragraphs, all correct. She raised her hand when Mr. Reyes called her name.

She read slowly, saving the best part. When she reached the log, the room got quiet. Marcus, who sat in front and usually drew monsters during read-alouds, had actually put down his pencil. Claire's voice sped up. "The branches snapped back as she knelt. 'Come here, boy,' she called. 'It's okay.' Biscuit crept out and pressed against her legs." She stopped. That was the last line on the page, and it felt like landing a jump off a high wall.

Marcus's hand shot up. "What happened to the dog after that? Did she take him home? Did her mom find out she skipped piano to look for him?" Three other kids nodded. Marcus said, "You can't just stop. I'll boycott sharing day if people keep doing endings like that." A few kids laughed, but Claire's stomach dropped. She had spent all her time on the dialogue and the rescue, and she hadn't noticed that the story quit exactly when the exciting part was over.

She sat down and pulled out her notebook. Mr. Reyes was walking around checking drafts, so she tapped Marcus's shoulder. "You said what happened after. Is there a name for that part?" Marcus shrugged, but Priya behind them held up a checklist from the writing folder and pointed to the last two lines. Claire read them, then read them again. "Falling action and resolution," she said under her breath.

At lunch she added to her list, working through it line by line. After the climax, the falling action and resolution show the consequences of what happened and tie up the story's loose ends. Priya's question was still ringing in her ears, so Claire flipped to a clean page and started writing. "They walked home in the dark, Biscuit's leash wound twice around her wrist. Her mom was on the porch, and she was not smiling." Marcus leaned over from the next seat. "Now I want to know what the mom says."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Like terms can be combined before solving, so 2x + 3x becomes 5x, but 2x and 3 cannot be combined because one has a variable and one does not.
story:
The smell of whiteboard marker hung in the air of Room 12 as Noemie stared at the board. 3x + 4 = 19. She was supposed to do the same thing to both sides, like a scale that had to stay balanced, but the x kept hiding behind the numbers, refusing to show what it was worth.

"How do you know it balances if you can't see inside?" she asked her lab partner, Deshawn.

"You just trust it," he said, tapping his pencil. Deshawn wanted to beat his older brother, who had finished this worksheet in ten minutes flat. He was racing, and racing made him messy.

Noemie tried it anyway. Take 4 from both sides. 3x = 15. Divide both sides by 3. She whispered it aloud, feeling the balance of it, and wrote x = 5. She checked by putting 5 back in, and both sides came out 19, like two doors opening onto the same room. Something she couldn't see had been there the whole time, and she had dug it out.

Then came the next problem, and the trouble. Deshawn grabbed the marker and wrote 2x + 3x + 3 = 23. Under it, fast and confident, he scribbled 5x + 3 = 23, then kept going, but before that he had crossed something out. Noemie leaned over. His first line had said 2x + 3 = 5x, treating the lonely 3 as if it belonged with the x's.

"You combined the 3 with the 2x," she said.

"So? They're all smushed together on the same side."

"But they're not the same kind of thing." She picked up a handful of counters from the bin. Two red counters, then three more red counters. "Two x's plus three x's, that's five x's." She set down a single blue counter. "But this 3 is just a 3. You can't squish it in with the x ones. It's like adding apples to a mystery box."

Deshawn frowned at the counters. "The 2x and the 3x are like terms," he said slowly, as if remembering something. He tried combining the 2x and 3x first, leaving the plain 3 alone, then subtracted 3 from both sides and got 5x = 20. "So x is 4." He checked it, and his face split into a grin. He was still going to tell his brother he'd won.

At lunch, Deshawn pushed his tray across the table toward Noemie, offering half a cookie, a small payment that symbolized more than it looked. "My grandma," he said, "she's a retired teacher. I told her about the apples and the mystery box, and she asked me one thing. She asked, 'What does the x stand for?'"

"What did you say?"

"I said, I have no idea, but it's definitely not a 3."

Noemie laughed so abruptly that milk nearly came out of her nose. "Okay, but seriously. What does it stand for?"

Deshawn shrugged and bit into the cookie. "Grandma says that's the whole game. Find out what's hiding."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: When asking a stranger for directions, Spanish speakers usually use the polite usted, French speakers vous, and German speakers Sie, rather than the familiar form.
story:
Natalie had one day left before her grandmother flew in from Monterrey, and so far she could say exactly one full sentence in Spanish: "Tengo un perro pequeño que se llama Biscuit." She said it to the mirror, to the toaster, and to Biscuit himself, who wagged at anything with her voice attached to it. Her mother, who advocated loudly for family bonds whenever Natalie wanted to skip a call, had made her a deal: describe every person and pet in the house in full sentences by tonight, and she could pick the movie on Friday.

She was working on "Mi hermano Marcus tiene quince años y toca la guitarra mal" when Marcus wandered in eating cereal from the box. "You know what's weird," he said. "In French class we just learned you're supposed to say vous to strangers. Like, always. Madame Perrin made us practice it on the janitor and he looked so confused."

Natalie wrote that down, mostly to make him go away. Then she texted her friend Priya, who took German on weekends, and Priya sent back a single message: "Sie. Same thing. My teacher says you'd sound like a toddler without it." So French had vous, German had Sie, and Natalie had a suspicion her Spanish book was hiding the same rule somewhere. The book only said usted meant "you," which was spectacularly unhelpful, since tú also meant "you." Two words, one meaning, no explanation. There had to be a pattern, and nobody was going to hand it to her.

The doorbell rang before she could stew on it. On the porch stood a small older woman in a raincoat, holding a handwritten address that had clearly survived a washing machine. "Busco Maple Street," she said. "Perdón, ¿dónde queda?"

Here it was: a stranger, a real one, asking directions, and Natalie's mouth was already loading the familiar tú she used with Marcus and Biscuit. She caught it mid-launch. Testing time. "Queda a dos cuadras, señora," Natalie said. "¿Usted busca la casa azul?" The woman's whole face did something warm and unhurried, like a cat settling into sun. She talked for a full minute about her granddaughter, the weather in Guadalajara, and the terrible numbering on Maple Street, and Natalie understood maybe half of it and nodded at all the right gaps. When she left, the woman squeezed her arm and said, "Qué niña tan educada."

Natalie closed the door and stood there feeling extremely spontaneous, in a planned and rehearsed sort of way. Then she went back to the kitchen, erased half her sentence list, and rewrote every line for her grandmother in the usted form, out loud, while Biscuit supervised from the warm spot by the fridge. "Mi abuela llega mañana," she told him. "Ella es la persona más terca que yo conozco." Biscuit yawned. From the hallway, Marcus called, "Was that Spanish or did you hurt yourself?"

"Usted no entiende nada," she called back.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Hostile attribution bias is the tendency to assume someone meant to hurt you when what they did was unclear or could easily have been an accident.
story:
Theo had been looking forward to Marcus's birthday sleepover for three weeks, and then Marcus's elbow knocked Theo's slice of pizza straight off the table and onto the carpet. "Nice one," Theo said, loud enough for everyone to hear. Marcus laughed with the other guys, and Theo decided, right there, that it was on purpose. Marcus had been showing off all night, taking the good controller, hogging the VR headset. This was just the newest move.

He spent the next hour collecting evidence. When Marcus passed the popcorn bowl past him to Dev, that was a snub. When Marcus picked Theo last for the Halo team, that was an insult. Theo's awareness of every little slight felt acute, like a radio tuned to one station: everything Marcus did, Marcus did to him.

At two in the morning, the guys were asleep and Theo was still awake, staring at the glow-in-the-dark stars on Marcus's ceiling. He started to replay the pizza moment, frame by frame, like rewinding a video. Marcus had been reaching across for the garlic knots. His chair legs had squeaked sideways just before his elbow moved. Had Marcus even been looking at Theo? He hadn't. His eyes were on the food. Theo sat up. Maybe he had tested the wrong theory the whole night. His simple idea: rerun each "insult" and ask one question, was there another possible cause? Popcorn bowl: it was on Dev's side. Halo teams: Marcus was balancing skill levels, and Theo actually stunk at Halo. Every clue had a second explanation.

At breakfast, Theo watched Marcus get up for juice, and Marcus's sneaker skidded on a patch of floor near the counter. "Whoa," Marcus said, arms windmilling, and Theo noticed a faint slick spot, probably from the pizza grease tracked off the carpet the night before. It was two feet from the table. Right where a chair pushing back could lose its grip.

"Marcus," Theo said. "Last night. The pizza. Did you slip?"

Marcus set the juice down. "Dude, yeah. My chair totally skated on something. I was going for the knots. Why, you thought I did it on purpose?"

"Maybe," Theo admitted. "Everything you did all night seemed aimed at me. I kept assuming you meant it."

"That's called hostile attribution bias," Marcus said, grinning. "My sister says I have it about my math teacher."

Theo laughed so hard he nearly choked on his waffles. "Okay, but in my defense, you were being annoying about the headset."

"I'll share the headset," Marcus said, sliding the last waffle onto Theo's plate. "Frontier day, my turn to explore new planets. You call shotgun on the goggles."

"Deal," said Theo, and grabbed the syrup.

fact: One of the first written guides to online manners, 'Netiquette Guidelines', was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855.
story:
"Delete it," Marcus said, hovering over Nicholas's shoulder. "Delete the whole group chat before Mr. Herrera sees it."

On the screen, the new class chat was already on fire. Someone had posted forty-seven crying-laughing emojis about Mr. Herrera's mustard-stained tie, someone else had replied in ALL CAPS, and Danny had nominated himself "Supreme Chat Overlord" in a message that scrolled for three paragraphs. Nicholas scrolled slowly, like a person watching a nature documentary. "Did you notice how everyone writes differently in here than they do out loud? Danny whisper-talks in class. In the chat he's basically shouting."

Marcus groaned and dropped onto the beanbag. "That's not the problem. The problem is Mr. Herrera made the chat for the volcano project, and now it's a volcano."

Nicholas kept scrolling, and a question started forming, the kind that itched. Had anyone ever written actual rules for this? Not school rules, but manners, the online kind? He typed it into the search bar while Marcus built a sandwich of suspense, saying nothing, just raising one eyebrow and waiting.

The results loaded. Nicholas blinked. "Okay, this is real. Somebody did write it down. It's called the 'Netiquette Guidelines,' and it was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855."

"RFC?" Marcus peered at the phone, a chip halfway to his mouth. "That sounds like a robot's gym locker."

"Probably some official document thing," Nicholas said, scrolling. The old text talked about not shouting in capitals, thinking before you post, remembering a real human reads your words. It was written before group chats even existed, back when phones had cords, and yet it described Danny exactly. Nicholas laughed out loud. "This guy predicted Danny in 1995. That's twenty years before Danny."

"So what do we do, print it and tape it to his locker?"

Nicholas was already typing, borrowing the old rules and rewriting them in Danny's own language. He posted: "Chat Constitution, Article 1: no caps unless spontaneous genuine screaming. Article 2: three emojis maximum. Article 3: volcanoes only."

The chat went quiet. Then Danny appeared in the doorway of Marcus's kitchen, still holding his phone, wearing the expression of a Supreme Chat Overlord who had just discovered he could be overthrown. "Article 2 is tyranny," he said. "I demand a rewrite."

"Nominate yourself to the rules committee," Nicholas said, and held up the phone so Danny could see the yellowed 1995 document on the screen. Danny leaned in, squinted, and read the title twice.

"Wait," he said. "They had internet manners before I was born and nobody told me?"

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: On a shaded sphere, the highlight is the brightest spot, on the side facing the light, and its position shows where the light is coming from.
story:
Max stood in front of a painting of a narrow street at the city gallery, his sketchbook clamped under one arm, scowling. His homework was to draw a street using one-point perspective, where every line ran toward a single vanishing point, and his version at home looked like a street designed by a dizzy giant. He had a letter from his art teacher folded in his pocket, and he pulled it out and read it again. "Max," it said, "go find the museum's oldest street painting. Find the point where the buildings' edges would meet if you extended them with a ruler. Then look at the round things. The lamp, the fruit cart, the boy's ball. If a sphere is shaded, the highlight is the brightest spot, and it sits on the side facing the light. Its position shows you where the light is coming from. Copy that, and your street will stop looking flat."

The painting, he discovered, was in a room with a skylight, and it did have a fruit cart with an orange on it. Max found the vanishing point first, tracing the building edges with his pencil in the air until they all aimed at a spot on the far door of the street, like the whole town was sliding toward it. Then he looked at the orange. It had one bright dab of paint on its upper left side, brighter than anything else on it. He held up his pencil as a pretend lamp, imagining the light arriving from exactly there, and checked a marble on the cobblestones nearby. Brightest spot, upper left. The cart wheel's rim caught its shine on the upper left too. It was a rule hiding under the paint, invisible until you hunted for it, and now Max saw little spotlight dots everywhere, like the street was secretly lit by a guild of tiny invisible lamplighters, all standing in the same corner of the sky.

"Excuse me," said a girl beside him, maybe ten, holding her own sketchbook open to a gray circle that looked like a flat gray cookie. "Mine's supposed to be a sphere but it looks like a blob. The docent said I should shade it, but I don't know where."

"Which side is the lamp on?" Max asked. He had decided to pretend he was a gallery wizard, since the skylight made everything glow anyway. "A sphere's highlight is the brightest spot, and it's on the side facing the light. So pick where your lamp is, and put your brightest spot there."

The girl bit her lip, jabbed a finger at the upper right of her circle, and drew one small brilliant dot. The blob popped into a ball so suddenly that she laughed out loud, and a guard three rooms away said "Shh" with impressive authority for someone so far away.

Max sat down on the gallery bench and started a fresh street. This time he drew the vanishing point first, aimed every roofline at it like roads to a castle, and gave each round thing, a lamp, a barrel, a bicycle bell, its brightest spot on the upper left, so that his whole imaginary street was lit by the same invisible sun. He was halfway through when the girl leaned over and said, "Your street looks nutritious enough to eat," and Max, who had been thinking of it as a place, had to admit that a street you could eat was even better, so he added a bakery with round golden loaves in the window, each with one bright spot, upper left, shining.

fact: Psychologist John Suler described the 'online disinhibition effect' in 2004: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face.
story:
The group chat had forty-seven messages by the time Simon sat down with his toast. It was the chat for the science fair, the one Mr. Okafor had set up, and someone had posted a photo of Maya's volcano display. Under it, from Priya's account, was a single line: "this looks like it was made by a third grader."

Simon read it twice. Priya was the girl who said "excuse me" to doors. She had lent him a pencil on Tuesday and thanked him for returning it as if he had done her a favor. He scrolled up and found three more sharp comments from her that week, each one public, each one aimed at somebody's project. In the hallway that same week she had complimented Maya's poster to her face. Simon had heard it himself.

He typed "why are you being so mean?" and then deleted it, because forty people would read it, and a public fight would just transport the whole mess somewhere worse. Instead he started a private chat. His assumption was that Priya would deny it, so he tested it with something small first. "Hey, was that you on the volcano comment?"

"obviously," she wrote back. "it's true. she glued the lava on crooked."

"Do you tell her that in person?"

There was a long pause, long enough for Simon to eat half his toast. Then: "no. that would be rude."

"Ruder than typing it?"

"typing doesn't count," Priya wrote, and Simon could almost see her shrug. He stared at the screen. It did count, though. The words were the same words; only the room was different.

He searched "why are people meaner online" and the first result was about something a psychologist named John Suler had described in 2004, called the online disinhibition effect: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face. Simon read it twice. That was it, exactly, Priya in one sentence. He pasted the link into the private chat.

A minute passed. Then Priya sent a single defiant "so???" followed by, "ok fine maybe the volcano comment was too much." In the main group chat, a new message appeared from her account: "hey Maya, the lava on your volcano is actually straighter than I said. sorry. also I found out my brain is broken in a normal way, ask Simon for the link."

Maya replied with a photo of her volcano wearing a tiny paper crown, and the caption "the third grader accepts your apology."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder, the Jewish meal retelling the Exodus from Egypt, the youngest able child traditionally asks the Four Questions.
story:
Christopher carried the folding chairs two at a time across the grass, because if he made three trips instead of five, he could get back to the pavilion before Aunt Ruth finished arranging the Seder plates. His family had claimed the corner of the park with the big oak trees, and long tables stretched under the branches where the Seder would happen, the whole meal that told the story of the Jews leaving Egypt, escaping from slavery under the pharaoh. "That pharaoh was like the worst landlord in history," Uncle Danny had joked that morning. "Wouldn't let his workers go no matter what." Christopher had laughed, then wondered what it would feel like to work for someone like that.

The real problem was Zoe. His cousin was seven, the youngest able child at the table, and all week she had been practicing the Four Questions on index cards she kept losing. She practiced them in the car, at breakfast, even once into the bathroom mirror while Christopher waited outside the door. At the Seder, the youngest one asks the Four Questions, and Zoe had whispered to him, "What if I freeze and everybody stares?"

He had an idea, and he wanted to test it before the meal started. His theory was that Zoe froze only when she felt alone, like the time she forgot her line at the school play. If she had someone to aim her words at, just one face instead of forty, maybe the words would come out fine. So while the grown-ups poured grape juice and set out the parsley and salt water, Christopher pulled two chairs behind the oak tree.

"Practice on me," he said. "Pretend everyone else is furniture."

Zoe narrowed her eyes at him. "Furniture doesn't eat karpas."

"Fine, very hungry furniture." She laughed, and then she asked him the first question, her voice wobbly at first, about how this night was different from all other nights. He noticed something: her hands stopped shaking when he nodded along, and by the third question she was looking straight at him, steady as a held note.

When the time came, the gradual fading of the afternoon light made the park smell like cut grass and someone's charcoal grill nearby. Aunt Ruth tapped her glass. Zoe stood up, and Christopher watched her scan the tables, watched panic flicker across her face, and then he caught her eye and gave one small nod, the exact nod from behind the oak tree. She took a breath, turned toward everyone, and asked all Four Questions without stopping once, her voice carrying past the tables toward the playground where kids on the swings went quiet to listen.

Afterward, Grandma Miriam squeezed Zoe's shoulder and said, "Some years these questions make me cry." Christopher bit into his matzah, which crumbled all over his shirt, and thought about how a person could grow like the oak overhead, thriving in good soil. Then Zoe plopped down beside him and whispered, "Same time next year?"

"Only if I'm still furniture," he whispered back.

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
knowledge_domain: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
fact: Perspective construction lines are drawn lightly, often with a hard pencil, so they can be erased once the room's real edges are darkened in.
story:
Laurence set her easel on the grass beside her cousin Dev, who had decided that anyone could paint a portrait in one afternoon. She had her grandmother's old box of watercolours, the pan nearly gone in the yellow corner, and a photograph of her grandmother propped against the fence. "You don't just draw it once," she said. "You start with the palest wash and let it dry, then add darker ones. Light to dark. You can't go backwards."

Dev frowned at his paper. He was more interested in the fence behind his drawing of the shed, and he had pressed so hard with his pencil that every guide line had carved a groove. "I'll just erase these later," he said.

Laurence remembered last winter, sitting at the kitchen table while her mother winced over a drawing of the living room. Her mother had pressed hard too, back when she was learning, and no eraser had lifted the lines. The finished room had stayed covered in them, faint rails running across the ceiling and floor, because the guide lines for perspective are drawn lightly with a hard pencil so they can be erased once the room's real edges are darkened in. Her mother had said, "You have to trust that the lines are there even when you can barely see them." Laurence had thought that was strange advice for drawing, and stranger still for everything else.

She laid her first wash, the palest peach, over the whole face and let the sun do the drying. While she waited she watched Dev scrub at his paper with the eraser until it pilled and tore. The grooves stayed. He flipped his board over, and she noticed the lines showed through the back, like bones under skin. "Try drawing the fence again on a fresh sheet," she said, "but press like you're drawing on a soap bubble."

Dev gave her the look he saved for advice from girls, the stereotype that art was her side of the family, some hereditary thing that had skipped him. But he picked up the hard 4H pencil she handed him and drew so lightly he had to tilt the sheet to see his own lines. "That's not drawing," he complained. "That's whispering."

"That's how it's supposed to look," Laurence said. She touched her brush to the second wash, a deeper rose along the jaw, and watched the first layer glow up through it. Dev leaned over her shoulder, holding his whispery fence up beside it.

"Okay," he said. "Teach me the faces next."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Emergency agencies advise unplugging computers and other electronics during a power cut, because a surge of electricity when the power returns can damage them.
story:
The lights went out at 8:40, right in the middle of Brooklyn's game, and the screen died to black. Her little brother Theo groaned from the couch. Their mom found the candles in the kitchen drawer, the ones shaped like pinecones that smelled like a fake forest, and set three of them on the coffee table. The flames leaned sideways whenever anyone walked past, throwing wobbly shadows up the wall.

"I was about to beat the whole level," Theo said.

"Beat it tomorrow." Brooklyn stared at the dark television. Then she remembered something her cousin Dev had told her last summer, after a storm knocked out power across his whole network of streets. He had lost his desktop computer that night. When the electricity came back on, he said, a surge of power had shot through the house and fried the machine. Emergency agencies told people to unplug their computers and other electronics during a power cut, because when the power returned, the surge could damage them.

"I didn't believe him at first," she said out loud, crouching behind the TV. "I thought he spilled juice on it and made up the surge thing." She pulled the console's plug from the wall and coiled the cord around her hand. Next she went to the desk in the corner and unplugged the desktop computer, then the router blinking dark on the shelf, then the microwave in the kitchen. Theo followed her with a candle, dripping wax onto a plate he carried like a waiter.

"What if the power comes back on while you're asleep?" he asked.

"That's the point. It can come back any time, and everything plugged in gets hit." She pointed at the lamp by the couch. "That one too, please."

The power stayed off until after 10. They played shadow puppets on the ceiling, and Theo made a shape he claimed was an authentic wolf, though it looked more like a rabbit with big ears. Brooklyn drew a map of the neighborhood in her notebook, trying to depict which streets might be dark, guessing it was just their block since the kitchen window showed lights glowing two houses down.

At 10:20 the ceiling fan spun once, the lamps blazed on, and the refrigerator started humming in the kitchen. The television screen stayed black and quiet, its plug lying on the floor where Brooklyn had left it. She smiled at it, then went around the room picking up her candles.

"Tomorrow, level twelve," Theo said. "Nobody fried."

"Nobody fried," Brooklyn said, and blew out the last pinecone.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In the 2020 NFL season, when most games had few or no fans because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1, showing no significant home advantage.
story:
The bleachers smelled like hot dogs and cut grass, and Violet's whole family had claimed the middle rows for the championship game between the Riverside Rockets and the Northside Bears. Her uncle Marco was already hoarse from yelling, and the game had not even started. "The crowd wins games," he kept shouting, drumming his fists on the railing. "That's the whole point of home field!" Violet frowned. She wanted the Rockets to win, and she wanted to believe Uncle Marco, but something about his claim bugged her, like a math problem with a step missing.

She thought back to two winters ago, when she had watched football at her grandmother's apartment during the year of the empty stadiums. The TV had shown rows and rows of vacant seats, and the games had felt strange and quiet, like a forest with no birds. Grandma had read the season totals out loud from her newspaper at the time, and the numbers had stuck in Violet's head ever since. She pulled out her phone now and searched until she found the page again, just to be sure.

"Uncle Marco," she said, tugging his sleeve during a timeout. "You know the season when almost nobody was allowed in the stadiums? Home teams finished 127 wins, 128 losses, and one tie. There was basically no home advantage at all." Marco blinked at her. Her cousin Jayden leaned over. "Wait, so cheering does nothing?" Violet shrugged. "It did nothing that year, at least. Maybe it's something else about home field. Maybe it's the players, not us." Marco looked wounded, like she had told him his cooking was bad. "Fine, science girl," he said. "Test it. Next few plays, nobody cheers. Then everybody goes wild. See what happens."

Violet felt a little thrill. An experiment, right here in the bleachers. She asked the families around them, and even a man with a foam finger agreed to stay silent for the next three plays. The stadium went oddly quiet, and the Rockets gave up a sack. Then she raised both arms, and the whole section erupted. The next play, the Bears intercepted the ball anyway. Marco threw up his hands. "That proves nothing!" Jayden laughed. "You need way more plays than that. That's the point, isn't it? One moment can't tell you anything." Violet nodded. Three plays was noise, not a pattern.

So they kept going, quiet then loud, loud then quiet, marking each result in her notebook, and by the fourth quarter she had a messy little chart that proved absolutely nothing except that the Rockets were aggressive on defense no matter what the crowd did. When the final interception sealed the win, Marco swept her up in a hug anyway. "All right," he admitted. "Maybe the cheering is for us." Violet grinned and waved her notebook above her head like a trophy. "Best data I ever salvaged from a blowout," she said, and Jayden said, "Save me a seat for the rematch."
